title: US to spend $400M for PH sea defense
summary: MANILA, Philippines — The United States said it will spend $400 million to strengthen the Philippine military’s operational reach and deterrence capability in the South China Sea as the two allies…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The United States said it will spend $400 million to strengthen the Philippine military’s operational reach and deterrence capability in the South China Sea as the two allies “pursue” a financing package of more than $2 billion to reinforce Manila’s defenses.

The US defense spending for its longtime Asian ally was announced on Wednesday by the White House at the end of US President Donald Trump’s state visit to Manila, where he also held a “special” summit with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean).

The White House said Trump announced that more than $17 billion in commercial deals and investments for US companies had been concluded during his visit. The financial agreements will also bolster regional security, protect the United States from “illicit activity” and support a “free and open” Indo-Pacific, it said.

The announcement comes as tensions escalate between the Philippines and China over their maritime dispute, especially in the West Philippine Sea, waters within Manila’s exclusive economic zone in the South China Sea.
The Philippines is a military ally of the United States, and the two countries have a longstanding Mutual Defense Treaty.

The White House said that part of the $400 million in military financing would support long-range firepower, command-and-control systems, critical infrastructure and drones capable of operating across multiple domains.

The two countries also agreed to supply the Philippines’ sovereign cloud infrastructure with trusted American “super intelligence” (SI) technology through the United States’ SI Exports Program. Super intelligence is the term Trump prefers for artificial intelligence.

The White House said that the Philippine Department of National Defense has a $37-million contract with a US company for technology-enabled mission support and has committed to working with American technology providers on a $63-million initiative to modernize its defense cloud infrastructure. The US companies were not identified.
The Philippines and the United States “will pursue a historic Foreign Military Financing (FMF) loan package” worth more than $2 billion, the White House said.
The White House did not disclose the proposed loan terms or a timetable for finalizing the package.

The Philippines will also modernize Basco Airport to improve operational access, disaster response and commercial supply chains in the country’s northernmost islands, according to the White House, which did not specify the amount to be spent.

The airport at Basco, the capital of Batanes province, is one of the nine sites across the Philippines that had been identified for use by US forces under the 2014 Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement between Manila and Washington.
Under the proposed FMF loan, the Philippines would acquire defense and security equipment from American suppliers.
The FMF program allows Washington to provide grants or loans to partner countries for the purchase of American defense equipment and services.
In December 2025, the US Congress passed a law authorizing up to $500 million a year in FMF grants for the Philippines from 2026 to 2030, or as much as $2.5 billion over five years.
The provision stemmed from a bipartisan bill introduced in April 2024 by US Senators Bill Hagerty and Tim Kaine. The funding, however, remains subject to congressional appropriations.

On trade, the White House said Trump and President Marcos committed to eliminating the US trade deficit with the Philippines through increased Philippine imports of American agricultural and energy products.
It did not specify the value or volume of the proposed imports, the products covered or when the commitments would take effect.
The announcement followed Trump’s claim that Washington had concluded its largest trade deal with the Philippines to date, although Philippine officials said no formal agreement had been signed.
Malacañang described the outcome as an understanding on areas of economic cooperation. Philippine Ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel Romualdez confirmed that no agreement had been signed.
The White House also said that Boeing and GE Aerospace have finalized a $12-billion sale of up to 20 Boeing 787 aircraft to Philippine Airlines. The planes will be equipped with GE Aerospace engines.

The Philippines and the United States also agreed to explore an intergovernmental agreement on civilian nuclear technology that could open opportunities for American companies to participate in the Philippine nuclear energy sector.

The White House said the US company Astranis announced that it was offering connectivity services from its US-manufactured Agila satellite to the Philippines, worth up to $200 million to provide independent and secure communications infrastructure for the Philippines.
It also cited plans by Subic Grain to construct a $40-million fuel storage depot at Subic Bay.

The White House said that Trump’s America First Arms Transfer Strategy underscored that the deals and proposed investments worth $17 million would support “tens of thousands” of American jobs, but there was no mention of jobs for Filipinos. /cb
